What begins as an intimate portrait of Russian independent journalists facing persecution by Putin’s regime takes a drastic turn when Russia starts a full-scale war in Ukraine and they are all forced into exile. The film offers a front row seat to how authoritarianism works and the lives of those who resist, which becomes all the more globally relevant every day.

Soviet-born American filmmaker Julia Loktev (The Loneliest Planet, Day Night Day Night) came to Moscow in 2021 to make a film about independent journalists being declared “foreign agents” by Putin’s regime - as it turns out, just four months before Russia started a full-scale war in Ukraine. With her friend Anna Nemzer, a talk show host at TV Rain, Russia’s last remaining independent news channel, Loktev brings us into a community of sharp, warm and funny young women speaking truth to power as they face increasing threats. Loktev filmed in Moscow during the first week of the full-scale invasion, as the journalists tried to counter Russian propaganda and report the truth on the war, until all independent media was shut down and they were forced to flee the country. Structured in five chapters, feeling like a cross between a Russian novel and a reality show about frighteningly real reality, Loktev’s film is an extraordinary historic record of a country on the verge of fascism and an immersive and intimate inside view of the opposition in an authoritarian society, which becomes all the more globally relevant every day.

Theatrical sneak peek!

A driven outsider penetrates Wu-Tang Clan's inner circle, channeling his ambition and creativity into an album that's about to spark worldwide controversy.

Wu-Tang Clan’s seventh studio album, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, was recorded in secret over six years, sealed in an ornate silver case, and first sold at a 2015 auction for a reported $2 million, under terms barring any commercial release until 2103.

In the years since, the record - and the story of how it came to be - has become the stuff of legend for hip-hop fans. Now, a new documentary on the album’s unlikely origins and controversial reception sets out to tell that story. After making its world premiere at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable, from Academy Award–winning filmmaker Joanna Natasegara, will arrive on Netflix Oct. 16.

The film follows Tarik Azzougarh - a Dutch-Moroccan Wu-Tang superfan performing as Cilvaringz - who talks his way into Wu-Tang Clan's inner circle and becomes the driving force behind the record at the center of the saga. What the MC and Wu-Tang set out to make was less an album than a provocation: a single, inimitable work of art conceived as a rebuke to a streaming era that had reduced music to disposable content - and built with full knowledge that it would court global controversy. Driving the project were two very different impulses: an appetite for a grand, potentially divisive gesture, and Wu-Tang Clan’s refusal to make anything less than a masterpiece.

The documentary marks Natasegara’s (The White Helmets, The Edge of Democracy) feature directorial debut. Abigail Anketell-Jones, Lauren Dark, and Vanessa Kirby produce.

Loktev filmed in Moscow during the first week of the full-scale invasion, as the journalists tried to counter Russian propaganda and report the truth on the war, until all independent media was shut down and they were forced to flee the country. Structured in five chapters, feeling like a cross between a Russian novel and a reality show about frighteningly real reality, Loktev’s film is an extraordinary historic record of a country on the verge of fascism and an immersive and intimate inside view of the opposition in an authoritarian society, which becomes all the more globally relevant every day.

A group of young journalists flee Moscow when Russia invades Ukraine and shuts down all independent media, turning telling the truth into a crime. Just days before, they were working as part of a vibrant opposition community. Now they’re part of a historic exodus. They leave with a few hours’ notice, carry-on suitcases, and no idea what country they can go to next that will let them stay and keep working. They must quickly get back on their feet to report on the biggest story of their lives, a war they all fiercely oppose. Intimate and immersive, the film sweeps across four years and a dozen countries. The complex, razor sharp and often very funny women - and a few men - gather in apartments that feel like waystations and borrowed offices before being uprooted yet again. They work to bring Russians an alternative to propaganda, speaking out against their country’s war crimes and wrestling with personal moral accountability, even as Russia menaces them with criminal prosecution back home and physical threats abroad. Relying on dark humor to get through dark times, they keep working for the uncertain future of a country they may not return to for decades. title.synopsis: The Story of Documentary Film traces the history of documentary from its very beginnings to the present day. Drawing on Mark Cousins’ decades of research, the series re-examines classics of the genre including Hoop Dreams, The Gleaners and I, Shoah, Stop Making Sense and Paris Is Burning. Structured chronologically, but interspersed with stand-alone thematic sections, the series challenges prevailing assumptions about what documentary is, offering a captivating new perspective on the history of a form that continues to shape how we understand the world around us.

title.name: Musk
title.synopsis: Elon Musk has amassed so much power, he’s like a character in a Marvel comic book. A short recap of his handiwork: Tesla popularized electric vehicles; Starlink expanded the reach of the internet; Twitter bowed to his takeover; and DOGE radically transformed the US government. Musk has been at the centre of AI development and this past summer, the IPO for SpaceX made him the richest man in the world. His influence arguably touches everyone on the planet. Surely this is worth fresh scrutiny. After nearly four years of work, Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney delivers his most ambitious and epic documentary, seeking to understand the history and motivations of the ultimate tech bro. When this film was first announced, Musk immediately denounced it on Twitter and refused to participate. But that didn’t impede Gibney, who draws upon countless hours of interviews that Musk has given over the years. Even more revealingly, Gibney conducts new interviews with figures who have known Musk up close and personal, including the mogul’s father, Errol Musk. The news cycle moves so fast, it’s hard to remember that Musk was once at home among liberals, with his companies promoting clean energy and invoicing the Obama administration for hundreds of millions in tech contracts. What drove him into the world of Donald Trump? Musk frequently invokes science fiction stories and has coyly wondered aloud if we’re living in a video game–like simulation. Playing off this idea, Gibney leans visually into an innovative graphic treatment throughout the film. But make no mistake: this is really happening.

title.name: Punishment Park
title.synopsis: Set during the Nixon administration, Punishment Park (1971) depicts a dystopian parallel reality in which detained political dissidents face an obscene decision. After being convicted of their “crimes” in a sham court proceeding, they are offered the choice between life in prison or three days in “Punishment Park,” a desert landscape where armed guards pursue them on foot as they race toward an American flag miles away on the dusty horizon. Those who can reach the flag before they are captured are promised release; those who are caught and refuse to comply with their captors’ demands are shot and killed. Peter Watkins’s staggering documentary-style drama moves across a barren landscape. Camera crews embed with the convicted men and women—and the armed forces chasing them—to expose these miscarriages of justice and their violent results. The film provokes us to consider the machinery of power and reflect on just how imaginary this imagined state is.

title.name: The Bend in the River
title.synopsis: The Bend in the River chronicles five close friends over nearly fifty years. Starting in 1978, director Robb Moss documents his friend’s outdoor rent-free life during one clothing-optional rafting trip through the Grand Canyon. In 2003, he filmed his friends again coming to terms with their transition from being young and carefree to responsible and middle-aged. Now, in 2025, Moss finds his friends in their 70s grappling with the choices they’ve made as individuals and as a generation. Cathy, Barry, Jim, Danny, and Jeff have lived most of their lives. They’ve held jobs, been married, had children, seen those children married, divorced, remarried, helped raise grandchildren, dreamt, suffered, succeeded and survived. The film interweaves moments from the distant past with those of the recent present, taking viewers back-and-forth through time and inviting candid reflections on what it means to live and grow old.

This exploration of both Barbara Hammer’s life, work, archive, and her ongoing legacy provides an urgent, necessary story of queer life, feminist history, and American cinema.

title.name: Soul Patrol
title.synopsis: Soul Patrol uncovers a hidden chapter of American military history by focusing on the Vietnam War's first Black special ops team, an elite unit operating deep behind enemy lines. With unprecedented access to this once-secretive group of African-American veterans, director J.M. Harper reconstructs their journey with an immediacy rarely seen in Vietnam War storytelling, using raw Super 8 footage, photographs, and audio recordings from their personal archives. Opening on the war’s 50th anniversary, the surviving members reunite in a hotel that becomes a surreal liminal space, where memory, brotherhood, and unresolved trauma collide. As the men reflect on their experiences, the film interrogates the contradictions of fighting for freedom abroad while facing inequality at home. Winner of the Directing Award for U.S. Documentary at the Sundance Film Festival, Soul Patrol is not just a war story, but a reckoning – an intimate portrait of survival, memory, and the enduring cost of war on those asked to fight it.

Fifty years later, completed by Greaves’ son David, Once Upon a Time in Harlem has emerged as a rapturous living archive of one of the most important artistic movements of the 20th century and, posthumously, one of the most important works in the Greaves filmography.

showtimes.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
showtimes.infoHtml:

One afternoon in August 1972, at the behest of legendary, genre-defying filmmaker William Greaves, a coterie of luminaries from the Harlem Renaissance gathered - with cameras rolling - for an intimate party in Duke Ellington’s townhouse. Fifty years later, completed by Greaves’ son David, Once Upon a Time in Harlem has emerged as a rapturous living archive of one of the most important artistic movements of the 20th century and, posthumously, one of the most important works in the Greaves filmography. 

A towering constellation of artists, poets, painters, musicians, scholars, and other notables appear throughout — among them Aaron Douglas, Arna Bontemps, Richard Bruce Nugent, James Van Der Zee, and Countee Cullen’s widow, Ida Mae Cullen. Free from any institutionalized gaze and structure, they congregate around a large punch bowl to drink, reminisce, banter, and passionately debate their legacy. The conversations we’re privy to flow naturally and candidly, marked variously by humour, fervour, reflexive insight, and not a bit of melancholy, as they take stock of their achievements in their older age.

Greaves’ multiple 16mm cameras are at the heart of the action, capturing and partaking in the collegial repartee, while the deft, contemporary editing balances the original ’70s textures with an exhilarating, contemporary immediacy, tracing the urgency of these artists and their ideas from the 1920s through to the 1970s and to our present moment.

Functioning as well as a dynamic inquiry into the ways culture is actively inherited and sustained across disciplines, and creates communities of protest and survival, Once Upon a Time in Harlem is a monumental reclamation of cinematic and cultural memory.

Marie-Lou (Efira) is the director of a nursing home in the Parisian suburbs and a devotee of an approach of caring for others, especially those with Alzheimer’s and dementia, called Humanitude, which requires continuous presence and risks the dangers of a more dynamic care unit. Her friendship with Mari (Okamoto), an avant-garde theater director, deepens her commitment to re-imagine elder care from a kinder, gentler place, resistant to the pressures to make the work fast and efficient and the patients docile and compliant.
